# Appendix C Deterministic and Two-Stage Stochastic MILP Implementations in Python and GAMS

## C1 From the planning problem to an executable model

The implementation follows the grain-storage formulation attributed to
@rosa2026thesis and presented in the main article. Facility opening and capacity
investment are chosen before supply and demand are realized. Grain movements,
inventory and the permitted shortages or capacity exceedances are then
determined for each operating trajectory. The purpose of this appendix is to
explain how those decisions are represented in software and how the resulting
calculations are checked. A reader can follow three successive questions:
which input arrays define the case (Appendix D), how the equations become
variables and constraints (Sections C2–C4), and what makes a returned answer
acceptable (Section C5). Section C7 provides one implementation index and a practical route through
public examples and the separate input-export procedure.

The deterministic (DET) and stochastic (STO) models use the same economic
objective and physical relationships. DET evaluates the original deterministic
supply and demand arrays. STO represents nine complete supply-demand
trajectories with a common investment vector and scenario-dependent operation.
The presence of 60 operating periods does not make this a multistage model:
the information structure has two decision stages.

Table C.1 relates the transport notation to the identifiers retained in the
implementation. In the legacy Python labels, D denotes the Portuguese
*depósito* (warehouse). This convention must be distinguished from topology D,
which permits direct origin-to-destination movements.

| Physical movement | Notation used in this appendix | Python label / GAMS variable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin to warehouse | OW | OD / xOW |
| Warehouse to destination | WD | DC / xWD |
| Warehouse to warehouse | WW | DD / xWW |
| Direct origin to destination | Direct OD | OC / xOD |

: Table C.1. Correspondence between physical transport families and implementation labels.

Topology W excludes direct OD movements; topology D permits them alongside
warehouse-mediated paths. Permission does not require positive direct flow.
The accepted evidence comprises nine W observations across h215–h500 and two
additional D observations at h215. The latter form a separate topology comparison,
rather than additional points in the warehouse-only scaling sequence.

## C2 Shared investment and scenario-dependent operation

The common implementation first prepares effective inputs and selects the
admissible product-specific network. It then creates opening, expansion and
bulk-handling decisions only for eligible facilities. Investment quantities and
their activation binaries have no scenario index. Operational flows, stock and
slacks are defined over the selected arcs, products and periods, with a scenario
index in STO. An absent arc has no decision variable.

This organization makes the distinction between stages explicit. Each scenario
uses the same installed capacity, while its operating decisions respond to its
own supply and demand. The objective charges investment once and takes the
probability-weighted sum of operating and penalty costs. Scenario probabilities
do not multiply material balances or capacity limits. A scenario's grain must
still satisfy the physical equations in its original units.

The following expression makes the shared-investment accounting explicit.
Let $W^N$, $W^X$ and $W^B$ denote candidate, expansion-eligible and
bulk-handling-eligible facilities; $O$, $W$ and $C^D$ denote origins,
warehouses and domestic destinations. Products and periods are indexed by
$P$ and $T$, and $S$ is the scenario set. The first-stage vector is
$X=(y,z,g,k,e,b)$: the first three entries are activation binaries and the
remaining entries are the corresponding investment quantities. For each
scenario, $Y^s$ contains arc flows $x$, end stocks $I$, domestic shortages $u$
and static/reception exceedances $q^K,q^R$.

The scalar objective and its fourteen components are

$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{X,\{Y^s\}}\ Z={}&C^{INV}(X)
+\sum_{s\in S}\pi_s
 \left[C^{TR}(Y^s)+C^{HOLD}(Y^s)+C^{PEN}(Y^s)\right],
\tag{C.1}\\
C^{INV}(X)={}&\sum_{w\in W^N}(F^N_wy_w+c^N_wk_w)
 +\sum_{w\in W^X}(F^X_wz_w+c^X_we_w)
 +\sum_{w\in W^B}(F^B_wg_w+c^B_wb_w),\\
C^{TR}(Y)={}&\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(o,w,p)\in A^{OW}}
 (f^O_o\ell^{OW}_{ow}+\tau_w)x^{OW}_{owpt}\\
&+\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(w,c,p)\in A^{WD}}f^W_w\ell^{WD}_{wc}x^{WD}_{wcpt}\\
&+\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(w,v,p)\in A^{WW}}
 (\alpha f^W_w\ell^{WW}_{wv}+\tau_v)x^{WW}_{wvpt}\\
&+\sum_{t\in T}\sum_{(o,c,p)\in A^{OD}}f^O_o\ell^{OD}_{oc}x^{OD}_{ocpt},\\
C^{HOLD}(Y)={}&\sum_{w\in W,p\in P,t\in T}h_{wp}I_{wpt},\\
C^{PEN}(Y)={}&\sum_{c\in C^D,p\in P,t\in T}\lambda^D_{cp}u_{cpt}
 +\sum_{w\in W,t\in T}(\lambda^K_wq^K_{wt}+\lambda^R_wq^R_{wt}).
\end{aligned}
$

In the component expressions, $Y$ denotes one scenario's operating vector.
Fixed investment charges $F$ are in BRL and quantity-dependent charges $c$
are in BRL per investment-tonne. Each transport coefficient combines a
distance $\ell$ in km and a freight rate $f$ in BRL/(t km), with a receiving
charge $\tau$ in BRL/t where applicable; $\alpha$ multiplies interwarehouse
freight. The holding charge $h$ is in BRL/(t period). The three $\lambda$
coefficients price their respective shortage, stock-exceedance and
reception-overflow quantities at each period. The scenario weights satisfy
$\sum_s\pi_s=1$. Stock and period throughput consequently enter different
physical checks even when both are measured in tonnes.

For DET, the original arrays are embedded as one scenario with probability one.
The resulting solution is projected back to the deterministic output format.
Thus, DET is neither the solution for a conveniently selected STO realization
nor a solution for scenario-averaged data. This specialization is also useful
for verification: a one-scenario STO case and its DET counterpart should agree
on objective components and feasibility, allowing for alternative optimal
decision vectors.

The physical equations are implemented in a corresponding sequence. Supply
leaves each origin; warehouse inventory links successive periods; domestic
arrivals plus shortage satisfy demand; and exports remain optional within their
specified limits. Static capacity bounds stock, whereas reception and shipping
capacities bound period throughput after converting daily rates using operating
days. Static and reception exceedances have separate slacks. Shipping,
conservation and route eligibility remain hard constraints. For a closed
candidate, the emergency slacks must also be zero.

## C3 Native Gurobi and SCIP implementations

Gurobi uses a common extensive-form builder for DET and STO. Its cost construction
separates six investment components, four transport components, inventory
holding and three artificial penalties: fourteen components in total.
The scalar model uses one optimization call under the stated time allowance.

The SCIP backend uses PySCIPOpt to create its own variables, constraints,
indicator relationships and scalar optimization call. It shares algebraic
helpers for investment, capacity and costs with the Gurobi implementation;
calling these helpers does not create a Gurobi environment. Both native
implementations express the closed-candidate implication using indicators,
without an arbitrary finite upper bound on an active candidate's slack.

Table C.2 links the main formulation to the principal software components.
The software reading index in Section C7 identifies the implementations.
Original experiments retain their own executed versions.

| Main equations | Computational role | Principal implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1/S1 | Investment, operation and penalties | Investment/scenario cost builders and the scalar objective |
| D2–D3 | Eligible investment and effective capacities | First-stage constraints and static/reception/shipping expressions |
| D4–D6 / S2–S4 | Supply and inventory conservation | Scenario physical-constraint construction |
| D7–D8 / S5–S6 | Domestic service and export limits | Destination balance and upper-bound rows |
| D9–D10 / S7–S8 | Capacity and closed-candidate conditions | Capacity rows and native indicators |
| D11/S9 | Domains and shared decisions | Eligible first-stage keys and nonnegative recourse variables |

: Table C.2. Mathematical relationships and their implementation roles.

The extensive-form builders implement these relationships; the mathematical
input contract prepares the effective arrays, and the independent validator
reconstructs balances and costs from exported decisions. The worked example
below illustrates this separation without requiring a source-code lookup.

## C4 Pyomo and the bounded representation of candidate slacks

The Pyomo implementation
and its bound derivation
provide a common scalar formulation for Gurobi, SCIP and HiGHS.
It uses the same effective data, investment expressions and physical balances.
The principal representational difference concerns candidate emergency slacks.
The native model allows an open candidate's slack to be unbounded above.
A finite bound must therefore be justified mathematically, rather than selected
because it appears numerically large.

For scenario $s$ and period $t$, let $G_{st}$ denote total exogenous supply,
and let $I^0$ denote total initial inventory. Let
$\overline H_{wt}$ be a finite upper bound on warehouse $w$'s *period*
shipping capacity, obtained from the original daily rates, operating days and
maximum eligible investments. Ignoring mutual exclusion when calculating this
upper bound can only enlarge it. Define

$$
M^K_{st}=I^0+\sum_{\tau\leq t}G_{s\tau},
\qquad
M^R_{st}=G_{st}+\sum_{w\in W}\overline H_{wt}.
\tag{C.2}
$$

The first bound follows by summing warehouse balances. Interwarehouse flows
cancel, while deliveries to customers and other withdrawals are nonnegative.
Consequently, the stock at any one warehouse cannot exceed initial stock plus
cumulative supply. Since installed static capacity is nonnegative, the minimum
required static exceedance is also bounded by $M^K_{st}$.

The reception bound must account for circulation. Arrivals from origins cannot
exceed current exogenous supply. Arrivals from other warehouses are bounded
by their hard shipping capacities, even if grain traverses several warehouses.
Their sum therefore provides a valid upper bound on incoming interwarehouse
flow. Current supply alone would not provide such a bound.

For each candidate warehouse with opening variable $y_w$, Pyomo imposes

$$
0\leq q^K_{swt}\leq M^K_{st}y_w,
\qquad
0\leq q^R_{swt}\leq M^R_{st}y_w.
\tag{C.3}
$$

When the candidate is closed, these constraints reproduce the native zero-slack
implication. When it is open, take any feasible native physical and investment
decisions and reduce its slack to the minimum nonnegative excess required by
the corresponding capacity inequality. The bounds above contain that
representative. Conversely, any solution satisfying the bounded constraints
also satisfies the original native implication and the unchanged physical rows.

With nonnegative candidate slack coefficients and scenario probabilities,
reducing redundant slack cannot increase the objective. The two representations
therefore have the same physical/investment projection and optimal scalar value.
They do **not** have identical full feasible sets in the redundant slack
coordinates. Nor does the proof establish identical relaxations, numerical
conditioning or search behavior. This is the precise equivalence asserted by
the explicitly selected bounded_scalar_slacks_v1 policy. Intuitively, the
transformation removes unnecessarily large slack values while retaining a
representative of every feasible physical plan and investment vector. It does
not promise that two solver interfaces will explore the same search tree.

The implementation checks the proof's finite, nonnegative data conditions and
records the derived bounds' identity and scope. Gurobi and HiGHS use Pyomo's
APPSI interfaces. The SCIP transfer adapter
reads the same Pyomo linear expressions and creates the native SCIP variables,
objective and constraints through PySCIPOpt. It does not rebuild the problem
with a separate scientific formulation.

To compare inputs to these adapters, the
ordered algebra record
includes variable domains and bounds, objective coefficients and constant,
and constraint coefficients and bounds. Matching records describe the common
Pyomo algebra before solver transformations; they do not assert identical
presolved models. Construction, transfer, optimization and validation are
therefore measured separately. Public analytical and intermediate-size controls
test correctness and operational behavior, but do not predict h215 runtime
or memory. Large-instance interpretation must retain these formulation,
interface and resource scopes.

## C5 Checking a returned solution

Independent validation reconstructs the fourteen cost components and evaluates
the original physical and investment constraints from the exported decisions.
It uses absolute tolerance $10^{-5}$ and relative tolerance $10^{-8}$, together
with the explicit sparse-export rounding allowance. Local constraints are
examined individually; national balance alone is insufficient.

Three outcomes must remain distinct. A usable incumbent supplies decisions that
can be checked. An accepted incumbent also passes the independent residual and
cost checks. A quality-qualified result additionally meets the stated gap target
using a valid bound. A solver or scheduler status alone does not establish these
properties. When no usable incumbent is available, financial costs, service
levels and an incumbent-based gap are unavailable.

The common gap uses the incumbent objective in its denominator, whereas a
solver may use a different native definition. Both are retained with their
definitions. A small gap for the penalized total remains a statement about that
total; it is not a relative-accuracy guarantee for the financial subtotal or a
proof that nominal capacity and full service can be achieved without slack.

### An illustrative balance and objective check

Consider a teaching example with one product, one operating day, one origin,
one candidate warehouse and one domestic destination. Two scenarios have
probability $1/2$. A specified plan opens the warehouse and installs 5 t of
static capacity at BRL4/t. At that capacity, its reception and shipping rates
are each 15 t/day. Initial stock and fixed opening cost are zero. Table C.3
gives the plan's flows and the corresponding end stocks.

| Quantity (t within the period, except end stock in t) | Scenario A | Scenario B |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Supply and origin-to-warehouse flow | 10 | 14 |
| Domestic demand and warehouse-to-destination flow | 8 | 12 |
| End stock | 2 | 2 |
| Shortage / static exceedance / reception overflow | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |

: Illustrative scenario balances.

The warehouse balances are $0+10-8=2$ and $0+14-12=2$. End stock is below
5 t, and each scenario's receipts and shipments are below the daily
handling limits. A free terminal-stock policy permits the remaining 2 t.
The example demonstrates checks on a specified feasible plan.

If each transport leg costs BRL1/t, receiving has no additional charge and
holding costs BRL1/(t period), the operating totals are
$10+8+2=20$ and $14+12+2=28$ BRL. Shared investment costs $5(4)=20$ BRL,
so Equation C.1 gives $20+(20+28)/2=44$ BRL. The validator checks the two
balances separately and reconstructs the same investment, transport and
holding totals. These illustrative values explain the accounting procedure;
the experimental input values are reported in Appendix D.

## C6 GAMS translation and verification limits

The supplement provides
model_det.gms and
model_sto.gms
as entry files, with
model_common.inc
containing the shared objective, constraints and domains.
The data-only exporter
writes already prepared effective Python inputs to data.inc and
produces an identifier and checksum record. This avoids manual transcription
of the large arrays while retaining the mapping to original facilities,
products, periods and scenarios.

The translation supports the declared scalable-candidate, daily-handling-factor,
free-terminal and three-enabled-slack configuration. Unsupported settings are
rejected. Closed-candidate indicators require the solver-specific mapping
described by [GAMS](https://www.gams.com/latest/docs/UG_LanguageFeatures.html#UG_LanguageFeatures_IndicatorConstraints);
omitting that mapping would change the model. The provided source does not
replace it with an arbitrary slack bound.

Structural inspection and exporter tests examine indexing, units, costs,
scenarios and input preservation. **The GAMS translation has not been compiled
or numerically validated.** Numerical verification requires comparing objective
components and original-unit residuals on the same small input; alternative
optimal decision vectors can represent the same scalar value.

: Implementation and verification index.

The index separates data preparation, model construction, solver transfer and
validation. A reader can therefore follow one physical relationship from its
effective input through the builder to the residual check, rather than treating
a solver's status as the complete numerical assessment.

Begin with the equations and the small accounting example above. In an
existing compatible Python environment, public input examples can be examined
with:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/test_excel_loader.py -q
```

Then obtain the exact processed workbook, population and network definition
described in Appendix D. Record the source, scenario design, solver/interface
settings and stopping rules for a fresh calculation. Validate the returned
decisions in original units, reconstruct all fourteen cost components and
compare the incumbent and bound using the declared gap definition.

For the GAMS translation, the exporter writes already prepared effective arrays
to data.inc and records identifier mappings and checksums in data_manifest.json.
Its inputs are a version-2 case manifest, a case index, a workbook and expected
hash, and a new output directory. The resulting data remain bound to that
workbook and case. The compilation and numerical-verification boundary is
stated in Section C6.
